clinicalPearls: Acquired grey-brown, often reticulate, pigmentation of the face and neck, classically over the forehead, temples and cheeks
Regarded as a form of pigmented contact dermatitis triggered by allergens in cosmetics, fragrances and dyes
Pigmentation may be preceded by mild erythema or itch before the discoloration becomes established
Patch and photopatch testing can identify the responsible allergen and guide avoidance
Histology shows a lichenoid/interface reaction with pigment incontinence and dermal melanophages
Identifying and avoiding the culprit allergen is central, with topical lightening agents and laser as adjuncts
The dermal component means Wood-lamp accentuation is limited and clearance is slow
reference.pathophysiology: Repeated low-grade allergic contact sensitisation to cosmetic ingredients provokes a lichenoid interface dermatitis at the dermoepidermal junction. Damage to the basal layer causes pigment incontinence, with melanin dropping into the papillary dermis where it is retained within melanophages. This dermal melanin produces the persistent grey-brown reticulate pigmentation that characterises the condition.
additionalInvestigations: Patch and photopatch testing to identify the causative allergen
Detailed cosmetic, fragrance and hair-dye history
Wood-lamp examination to gauge pigment depth
Skin biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: Failure to improve despite thorough allergen avoidance, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Features suggesting exogenous ochronosis from misuse of topical lightening agents
Widespread or systemic pigmentation pointing to a drug or internal cause
reference.prognosis: With identification and avoidance of the responsible allergen the pigmentation slowly improves over months to years, though some residual dermal pigment may persist.
pitfalls: Not undertaking patch testing and therefore missing the causative allergen
Confusing it with melasma and continuing the offending cosmetic
Allowing ongoing allergen exposure, which perpetuates the pigmentation
Expecting a rapid response from lightening agents against dermal pigment
management: Identify and avoid the culprit allergen through patch and photopatch testing, the central step in management
Discontinue the offending cosmetics, fragrances and hair dyes
Apply topical lightening agents such as hydroquinone or azelaic acid to fade the dermal pigment
Use Q-switched laser therapy as an adjunct for persistent pigmentation
Advise broad-spectrum photoprotection to limit further pigmentation
Reassure that pigmentation improves slowly over months to years once the allergen is removed
